questions.stem: Which change is an anthropogenic cause of climate change within the scope of D4.3?

options.text: Increased atmospheric carbon dioxide from fossil-fuel combustion
options.why: Combustion transfers carbon from long-term geological stores into the atmosphere as carbon dioxide, strengthening the greenhouse effect.

options.text: Increased incoming solar radiation caused by methane emissions
options.why: Methane affects the amount of outgoing infrared radiation retained by the atmosphere. It doesn't increase the Sun's energy output.

options.text: Reduced atmospheric oxygen caused directly by ocean acidification
options.why: Ocean acidification is caused by carbon dioxide dissolving in seawater. It isn't the direct cause of the enhanced greenhouse effect.

options.text: Increased geothermal heat released by combustion of coal and oil
options.why: Burning fossil fuels releases greenhouse gases. It doesn't cause Earth to release more geothermal energy.

questions.stem: Ice-core records show a positive correlation between atmospheric carbon dioxide and global temperature. What can be concluded from that result alone?

options.text: Higher carbon dioxide concentrations are associated with higher temperatures, but the data alone don't establish causation
options.why: A positive correlation shows that the variables tend to change together. Other evidence is needed to demonstrate the causal mechanism.

options.text: Higher carbon dioxide concentrations must be the only cause of every recorded change in global temperature
options.why: A correlation doesn't identify one exclusive cause. Other climate variables can also affect temperature.

options.text: Higher global temperatures must always cause carbon dioxide concentrations to decrease
options.why: That describes a negative relationship, while the ice-core variables show a positive correlation.

options.text: Carbon dioxide and temperature have no relationship because both changed before industrialization
options.why: Changes before industrialization don't erase the observed relationship. The records still show that the variables tend to rise and fall together.

questions.stem: Which sequence describes the ice–albedo positive feedback?

options.text: Warming melts ice, lowering albedo and increasing solar absorption, which causes further warming
options.why: Ice loss exposes darker surfaces that reflect less and absorb more incoming radiation. That added absorption amplifies warming.

options.text: Warming melts ice, raising albedo and increasing reflection, which causes further warming
options.why: Melting lowers albedo rather than raising it. Greater reflection would oppose warming instead of amplifying it.

options.text: Warming forms more ice, lowering sea level and increasing absorption, which causes further warming
options.why: Warming generally causes ice loss. Sea-level change isn't the mechanism in the albedo feedback.

options.text: Warming melts ice, releasing nutrients and increasing photosynthesis, which causes further warming
options.why: That mixes albedo with nutrient cycling. The relevant change is reduced reflection and increased absorption of solar radiation.

questions.stem: When has a boreal forest changed from a carbon sink to a carbon source?

options.text: When its carbon release exceeds its carbon uptake
options.why: A source has net carbon release. Drought, reduced primary production and fire can push the balance in that direction.

options.text: When its total stored carbon reaches its highest value
options.why: The size of the carbon store doesn't define the current balance. A large store may be gaining or losing carbon.

options.text: When photosynthesis exceeds respiration and combustion
options.why: That produces net carbon uptake, which defines a carbon sink rather than a source.

options.text: When snowfall increases and drought becomes less frequent
options.why: Those conditions don't describe the syllabus tipping-point mechanism. Warming, reduced snowfall and drought promote browning and fire.

questions.stem: Why can warmer surface water reduce marine primary production?

options.text: It strengthens stratification and reduces nutrient upwelling into the sunlit surface layer
options.why: Reduced vertical mixing leaves more nutrients in deep water. Phytoplankton at the surface then have fewer nutrients for growth.

options.text: It removes all mineral nutrients from seawater by increasing their rate of evaporation
options.why: Dissolved mineral nutrients don't evaporate with water. The problem is their location below the sunlit surface layer.

options.text: It increases vertical mixing and carries phytoplankton below the ocean floor
options.why: Surface warming tends to strengthen stratification and reduce mixing. Phytoplankton aren't carried below the ocean floor.

options.text: It prevents sunlight from entering water by increasing atmospheric carbon dioxide
options.why: The upwelling mechanism concerns nutrient supply, not carbon dioxide blocking sunlight from the ocean.

questions.stem: Which climate-change effect is correctly matched with the organism?

options.text: Early breakup of Antarctic landfast ice reduces emperor penguin breeding habitat
options.why: Emperor penguins use stable landfast ice for breeding. Early breakup can occur before chicks are ready to survive independently.

options.text: Loss of Arctic sea ice removes the nesting trees used by emperor penguins
options.why: Emperor penguins breed on Antarctic ice, not in Arctic trees. Sea ice loss in the Arctic is the walrus example.

options.text: Expansion of Antarctic landfast ice removes the feeding platforms used by walruses
options.why: Walruses live in the Arctic and are threatened by sea ice loss. Antarctic landfast ice is linked to emperor penguin breeding.

options.text: Ocean acidification melts the coastal ice used by both species for reproduction
options.why: Ice loss is driven mainly by warming, not acidification. The two species also use ice in different regions and ways.

questions.stem: What is the best explanation for an upslope range shift?

options.text: Conditions within a species' temperature tolerance occur at progressively higher elevations
options.why: As lower elevations warm, cooler suitable conditions may remain higher on the mountain, shifting population distribution upslope.

options.text: Every organism climbs uphill during its lifetime to avoid increased carbon dioxide
options.why: A range shift is a population-level distribution change. It isn't an identical behavioral response by every individual.

options.text: High-elevation habitats become warmer than low-elevation habitats during climate change
options.why: Higher elevations generally remain cooler than nearby lower elevations. Species shift upward to remain within suitable conditions.

options.text: Natural selection immediately changes every individual into a high-altitude species
options.why: Natural selection acts across generations and doesn't transform every organism. Range movement can occur without immediate evolutionary change.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes ocean acidification from coral bleaching?

options.text: Acidification suppresses calcification, whereas high temperature can cause loss of coral symbionts
options.why: Carbon dioxide lowers pH and reduces carbonate availability. Heat stress can cause the loss of photosynthetic symbionts or their pigments.

options.text: Acidification expels coral symbionts, whereas high temperature increases carbonate ion availability
options.why: This reverses both mechanisms. Heat stress causes bleaching, while acidification reduces carbonate availability.

options.text: Acidification immediately kills all corals, whereas bleaching always improves coral survival
options.why: Acidification suppresses calcification rather than killing every coral immediately. Bleaching reduces energy supply and can lead to death.

options.text: Acidification raises ocean pH, whereas bleaching forms carbonic acid inside coral skeletons
options.why: Acidification lowers pH. Bleaching concerns loss of symbionts or pigments, not carbonic acid formation inside the skeleton.

questions.stem: Why can restoring a peat-forming wetland sequester carbon?

options.text: Waterlogged conditions slow decomposition and allow organic matter to accumulate
options.why: Low oxygen availability limits decomposition, so partially decomposed material and its carbon can accumulate as peat.

options.text: Dry soil accelerates decomposition and converts carbon dioxide into peat
options.why: Drying exposes peat to oxygen and can increase decomposition. Carbon dioxide isn't directly converted into peat by decomposition.

options.text: Flooding causes all soil organisms to increase their rates of aerobic respiration
options.why: Waterlogging restricts oxygen diffusion, so aerobic decomposition generally slows instead of increasing.

options.text: Peat releases methane without storing any carbon in organic matter
options.why: Peat is a store of organic carbon. Methane production can occur, but it doesn't mean that no carbon is stored.

options.text: Recording the dates of budburst in the same tree population over many years
options.why: Phenology examines the timing of recurring biological events. A long record can reveal whether budburst timing changes.

options.text: Measuring the number of tree species found within a forest quadrat
options.why: That measures species richness in a community. It doesn't measure the timing of a recurring biological event.

options.text: Comparing the nucleotide sequences of two genes in one bird species
options.why: That investigates genetic variation. It doesn't concern seasonal timing such as migration or nesting.

options.text: Determining the trophic level occupied by caterpillars in a food chain
options.why: That concerns feeding relationships. Phenology would investigate when caterpillar biomass reaches its seasonal peak.

questions.stem: How can climate change disrupt phenological synchrony between two interacting populations?

options.text: Different environmental cues cause their seasonal events to shift by different amounts
options.why: One event may respond strongly to temperature while another depends more on photoperiod, producing a mismatch in timing.

options.text: The annual photoperiod cycle becomes longer as atmospheric temperature rises
options.why: Climate warming changes temperature patterns, but it doesn't lengthen the yearly pattern of day length at a location.

options.text: Every population responds identically because temperature controls all biological events
options.why: Populations can respond to different cues and at different rates. That difference is what allows synchrony to break down.

options.text: Both populations permanently stop reproducing after one unusually warm day
options.why: Phenological mismatch concerns shifts in relative timing, not an automatic permanent end to reproduction.

questions.stem: Why can reduced snow cover cause evolution in a tawny owl population?

options.text: Brown variants gain higher fitness, so associated alleles become more frequent over generations
options.why: Differential survival and reproduction act on heritable color variation. The resulting allele-frequency change is evolution.

options.text: Gray owls change their feathers permanently to brown during their own lifetimes
options.why: An individual doesn't change its inherited color variant in response to snow. The population changes across generations.

options.text: Reduced snow creates new brown alleles in every owl at the same time
options.why: The environment selects among heritable variants already present. It doesn't direct the same mutation in every individual.

options.text: Brown owls survive better, but their reproductive success and allele frequencies remain unchanged
options.why: A survival advantage affects evolution only when it contributes to differential reproductive success and changes heritable frequencies.
